lessons.title: Spark architecture: driver, executors, cluster manager
lessons.summary: A Spark application is one driver process plus many executor processes.
lessons.remember: The driver plans, the executors do the work one partition per task, and the cluster manager supplies the machines.

lessons.title: SparkSession, SparkContext and running locally
lessons.summary: SparkSession is the single entry point to Spark in modern code.
lessons.remember: SparkSession is the one door into Spark; SparkContext is the older, lower-level door it wraps.

lessons.title: RDD vs DataFrame (and a note on Dataset)
lessons.summary: Spark has three data abstractions: - RDD (Resilient Distributed Dataset): a distributed collection of arbitrary objects.
lessons.remember: In PySpark, use DataFrames; RDDs are a low-level escape hatch and Dataset is a Scala and Java idea.

lessons.title: Lazy evaluation: transformations and actions
lessons.summary: Spark operations come in two kinds: - Transformations (select, filter, join, groupBy, withColumn) return a new DataFrame and only add a step to a plan.
lessons.remember: Transformations build a plan; only actions run it, and every action runs it again unless you cache.

lessons.title: The DAG and RDD lineage
lessons.summary: When an action runs, Spark turns the optimised plan into a DAG (directed acyclic graph) of steps.
lessons.remember: Spark splits the DAG into stages at shuffles, and uses lineage to recompute lost partitions instead of keeping copies.

lessons.title: Schemas and data types
lessons.summary: Every DataFrame has a schema: an ordered list of column names, types and nullability, held as a StructType of StructFields.
lessons.remember: Declare schemas for text sources and use decimals for money; inference is a convenience, not a contract.

lessons.title: Columns, expressions, select and filter
lessons.summary: DataFrame code is built from column expressions.
lessons.remember: A column is an expression, not data; build logic from expressions so Spark can optimise it.

lessons.title: Working with nulls
lessons.summary: Spark SQL follows SQL's null rules: any comparison with null gives null, and a filter keeps only rows where the condition is true.
lessons.remember: Null is "unknown", so comparisons with it are never true; test for it explicitly and use null-safe equality where two unknowns should match.

lessons.title: Sorting, distinct, limit and sampling
lessons.summary: Four everyday operations with very different costs: - orderBy / sort produces a total order across all partitions.
lessons.remember: Global sorts and distincts shuffle everything; ask whether you need them before you write them.

lessons.title: groupBy, aggregation, rollup and cube
lessons.summary: groupBy(keys).agg(...) collapses rows with the same key into one row and computes aggregate expressions: sum, count, avg, min, max, countDistinct, collectlist, first, percentileapprox and many more.
lessons.remember: groupBy shuffles once and aggregates partially first; rollup and cube add subtotal rows marked by grouping().

lessons.title: Joins in Spark
lessons.summary: df.join(other, on, how) combines two DataFrames.
lessons.remember: Join on column names to avoid duplicate keys, use leftsemi and leftanti for existence checks, and watch for key duplication.

lessons.title: Union and set operations
lessons.summary: - union(other) appends rows by position.
lessons.remember: Use unionByName, not union, unless you have checked column order yourself.

lessons.title: Pivot and unpivot
lessons.summary: Pivot turns distinct values of one column into new columns, with an aggregate in each cell: groupBy("product").pivot("month").sum("qty").
lessons.remember: Pivot with an explicit values list; unpivot wide legacy tables into rows early.

lessons.title: Explode and nested data
lessons.summary: JSON, Avro and API data often contain arrays and nested structs.
lessons.remember: explode turns array elements into rows; use explodeouter to keep empty ones and never explode two arrays blindly.

lessons.title: Window functions in Spark
lessons.summary: A window function computes a value for each row from a window of related rows, without collapsing them like groupBy does.
lessons.remember: Windows compute per-row results over related rows; always state the frame when you mean rows, and partition by a key.

lessons.title: Deduplication patterns
lessons.summary: Two kinds of duplicates need two tools: - Exact or key duplicates where any copy will do: dropDuplicates("key") keeps one arbitrary row per key.
lessons.remember: dropDuplicates keeps any copy; when one copy must win, rank with rownumber and a full tie-breaking order.

lessons.title: Built-in functions: string, date, math, conditional
lessons.summary: pyspark.sql.functions (imported as F) holds hundreds of functions that run inside the JVM: - String: upper, trim, concatws, substring, split, regexpreplace, lpad, formatstring.
lessons.remember: Reach for pyspark.sql.functions first; a built-in is almost always faster than anything you write in Python.

lessons.title: Arrays, maps, structs, JSON and regex
lessons.summary: Spark handles nested data natively: - Structs group fields: F.struct(...) builds one, col("a.b") reads one.
lessons.remember: Parse JSON once with a schema, and use higher-order functions to work inside arrays without exploding them.

lessons.title: Python UDFs
lessons.summary: A user-defined function (UDF) runs your own Python function on each row.
lessons.remember: A Python UDF is a black box that ships every row to Python; use it only when no built-in or pandas UDF fits.

lessons.title: pandas UDFs and Apache Arrow
lessons.summary: A pandas UDF (vectorised UDF) receives whole batches of rows as pandas Series or DataFrames instead of one row at a time.
lessons.remember: pandas UDFs move data in Arrow batches, so Python libraries can run on Spark at near-vectorised speed.

lessons.title: Broadcast variables and accumulators
lessons.summary: Two shared-variable tools from the RDD era that still matter: - A broadcast variable sends a read-only value (a lookup dictionary, a small model) to every executor once, instead of with every task.
lessons.remember: Broadcast ships read-only data once per executor; accumulators in transformations can over-count on retries, so do not use them for exact business numbers.

lessons.title: Spark SQL, views, subqueries and CTEs
lessons.summary: Spark SQL and the DataFrame API are two front ends to the same engine.
lessons.remember: SQL and DataFrames compile to the same plan, so pick whichever reads better for each step.

lessons.title: Catalog, databases and tables
lessons.summary: Spark keeps table definitions in a catalog (metastore).
lessons.remember: Managed tables let the catalog own the files; external tables only point at them, and modern catalogs add a third naming level.

lessons.title: Query hints
lessons.summary: Hints tell the optimiser to choose a plan it might not choose itself.
lessons.remember: Hints override the optimiser; use them for proven problems and revisit them when data volumes change.

lessons.title: Reading and writing data, save modes
lessons.summary: spark.read returns a DataFrameReader: you set format, options and an optional schema, then load a path or table.
lessons.remember: Readers set format, options and schema; writers set format and mode, and only a table format makes overwrite safe.

lessons.title: File formats: CSV, JSON, Parquet, ORC, Avro, and compression
lessons.summary: - CSV: text, row-based, no types, many dialects.
lessons.remember: Land raw data in whatever the source gives you, but store analytical data in a columnar format, usually Parquet under a table format.

lessons.title: XML and Excel files
lessons.summary: Legacy systems often hand over XML or spreadsheets.
lessons.remember: XML is readable natively in Spark 4 (via spark-xml before), while Excel is a small-data, driver-side job.

lessons.title: JDBC reads and writes
lessons.summary: Spark reads from and writes to relational databases through JDBC.
lessons.remember: A JDBC read is single-threaded until you give it a partition column or predicates, and every partition is another connection to the source.

lessons.title: Partitioning and bucketing on disk
lessons.summary: Partitioning on disk (df.write.partitionBy("country", "loaddate")) writes one folder per value: .../country=DE/loaddate=2025-10-15/.
lessons.remember: Partition on disk by a low-cardinality filter column such as date; too many partitions is worse than none.

lessons.title: Partitions, repartition and coalesce
lessons.summary: A DataFrame is split into partitions: chunks of rows processed independently, one task per partition.
lessons.remember: Partitions set parallelism; repartition shuffles to rebalance, coalesce merges cheaply but only downward.

lessons.title: Shuffle
lessons.summary: A shuffle redistributes rows across partitions so that rows with the same key end up together.
lessons.remember: A shuffle moves rows by key across the network between stages; filter and project before it, and avoid the ones you do not need.

lessons.title: Data skew
lessons.summary: Skew means some keys have far more rows than others.
lessons.remember: Skew is one key with too many rows; check nulls and hot keys, let AQE split joins, broadcast if possible, and salt as a last resort.

lessons.title: Caching and persistence
lessons.summary: Because every action re-runs the plan from the source, a DataFrame used several times is computed several times.
lessons.remember: Cache only what you reuse, materialise it with an action, and unpersist when done.

lessons.title: Broadcast joins and join strategies
lessons.summary: Spark picks a physical join strategy for each join: - Broadcast hash join: the small side is collected and sent to every executor; each task joins its partition of the large side locally.
lessons.remember: Broadcast the small side to avoid shuffling the big one; sort-merge is the safe default for two large tables.

lessons.title: Adaptive Query Execution
lessons.summary: Adaptive Query Execution (AQE), on by default since Spark 3.2, re-optimises a query while it runs, using real statistics collected at each shuffle boundary rather than estimates made before the start.
lessons.remember: AQE re-plans at each shuffle using real sizes: it merges small partitions, switches to broadcast joins, and splits skewed join partitions.

lessons.title: Catalyst optimiser and Tungsten engine
lessons.summary: Every DataFrame or SQL query passes through Catalyst, Spark's optimiser, in four phases: 1.
lessons.remember: Catalyst rewrites and plans the query, Tungsten executes it with compact memory and generated code.

lessons.title: Reading explain plans
lessons.summary: df.explain(mode) prints the plan Spark will run.
lessons.remember: Read plans bottom-up and look at scans for pushed filters, Exchanges for shuffles, and join operators for the strategy.

lessons.title: Partition pruning, column pruning and predicate pushdown
lessons.summary: The fastest data to process is data you never read.
lessons.remember: Filter on stored columns, select only what you need, and lay data out so statistics can skip files.

lessons.title: Memory, spill and garbage collection
lessons.summary: Each executor's JVM heap is divided by Spark's unified memory manager into: - Execution memory: buffers for shuffles, joins, sorts and aggregations.
lessons.remember: Spill means partitions are too big for execution memory; out-of-memory means something could not spill, often skew, collect, broadcast or Python.

lessons.title: Jobs, stages, tasks and the Spark UI
lessons.summary: The vocabulary of Spark execution: - Job: what one action triggers.
lessons.remember: An action is a job, shuffles split it into stages, each stage runs one task per partition, and the Spark UI shows where time went.

lessons.title: Delta Lake: ACID tables on files
lessons.summary: Plain Parquet folders have no transactions: a failed write leaves half-written files, readers can see partial results, and you cannot update a row.
lessons.remember: Delta adds a transaction log to Parquet files, giving ACID writes, schema enforcement, MERGE and time travel on a data lake.

lessons.title: MERGE and upserts in Delta
lessons.summary: MERGE INTO combines insert, update and delete in one atomic operation, driven by a join between a source (new or changed rows) and the target table: - WHEN MATCHED AND condition THEN UPDATE SET ...
lessons.remember: MERGE applies inserts, updates and deletes atomically from a deduplicated source; limit the target files it touches.

lessons.title: Time travel, restore and vacuum
lessons.summary: Because Delta never overwrites files in place, older versions of a table remain readable: - Time travel: SELECT FROM t VERSION AS OF 12 or TIMESTAMP AS OF '2025-10-01', or the versionAsOf reader option.
lessons.remember: Delta keeps old versions until VACUUM removes files beyond the retention window; use time travel as undo, not as backup.

lessons.title: Compaction, Z-order and liquid clustering
lessons.summary: Two layout problems slow down Delta tables: 1.
lessons.remember: Compact small files with OPTIMIZE, and cluster on the columns you filter by, preferring liquid clustering for new tables.

lessons.title: Schema enforcement and evolution
lessons.summary: Schema enforcement: Delta rejects writes whose columns or types do not match the table, instead of silently corrupting it.
lessons.remember: Delta enforces the schema by default; allow evolution deliberately, mostly in raw layers.

lessons.title: Change data feed
lessons.summary: The change data feed (CDF) records row-level changes made to a Delta table.
lessons.remember: Change data feed exposes each row's insert, update and delete since a version, so downstream jobs process only changes, including deletes.

lessons.title: Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi
lessons.summary: Delta is one of three widely used open table formats.
lessons.remember: Iceberg is the most engine-neutral format with catalog-based metadata, Hudi targets upsert-heavy pipelines, and Delta dominates Spark-centred platforms.

lessons.title: Slowly changing dimensions in Spark
lessons.summary: A slowly changing dimension (SCD) is a dimension table (customer, product) whose attributes change over time.
lessons.remember: SCD type 1 overwrites, type 2 closes the old row and inserts a new one, and in Delta both are MERGE statements.

lessons.title: Medallion architecture
lessons.summary: The medallion architecture organises lakehouse data into layers of increasing quality: - Bronze (raw): data as received, append-only, with ingestion metadata (source file, load time).
lessons.remember: Bronze keeps raw history, silver cleans and conforms, gold serves the business; the value is in clear responsibilities, not the names.

lessons.title: What Microsoft Fabric is
lessons.summary: Microsoft Fabric is a SaaS analytics platform.
lessons.remember: Fabric is one SaaS platform where every workload shares a capacity for compute and OneLake for storage.

lessons.title: OneLake
lessons.summary: OneLake is the single logical data lake that comes with every Fabric tenant.
lessons.remember: OneLake is one ADLS-based lake per tenant, organised by workspace and item, holding Delta tables that every Fabric engine reads.

lessons.title: Tenants, capacities and workspaces
lessons.summary: Fabric has a four-level containment hierarchy: 1.
lessons.remember: Tenant holds settings and OneLake, capacities supply regional compute, workspaces hold items, and domains group workspaces for governance.

lessons.title: Licensing and capacity units
lessons.summary: Fabric is paid mainly through capacities.
lessons.remember: You buy capacity units that every workload shares; bursting and smoothing absorb spikes, and sustained overuse leads to staged throttling.

lessons.title: Fabric vs Synapse, ADF and Power BI Premium
lessons.summary: Fabric is Microsoft's successor platform for several earlier services: - Azure Synapse Analytics: Fabric Data Warehouse, Fabric Spark, pipelines and Eventhouse cover the same ground as dedicated SQL pools, Synapse Spark,
lessons.remember: Fabric absorbs Synapse, ADF and Power BI Premium, but the mapping is not one-to-one and moving is a project, not a switch.

lessons.title: Lakehouse
lessons.summary: A Lakehouse is a Fabric item that stores data in OneLake and is designed to be written mainly by Spark (notebooks, Spark job definitions) and by Data Factory.
lessons.remember: A Lakehouse is Spark-first storage with a Files area for anything and a Tables area of Delta tables that every Fabric engine can read.

lessons.title: Warehouse
lessons.summary: A Fabric Warehouse is a relational data warehouse you build and load with T-SQL.
lessons.remember: The Warehouse is the T-SQL-first, read-write store in Fabric, with multi-table transactions and Delta storage underneath.

lessons.title: SQL analytics endpoint
lessons.summary: The SQL analytics endpoint is a read-only T-SQL interface that Fabric creates automatically for each lakehouse, mirrored database and SQL database (exactly one per item).
lessons.remember: The SQL analytics endpoint gives read-only T-SQL over lakehouse tables, with a sync delay and with security that protects only the SQL path.

lessons.title: Shortcuts
lessons.summary: A shortcut is a pointer in OneLake to data stored somewhere else.
lessons.remember: A shortcut is a zero-copy pointer to data elsewhere; external shortcuts read with a shared delegated credential.

lessons.title: Mirroring
lessons.summary: Mirroring continuously replicates data from an operational or analytical source into OneLake as Delta tables, without you building pipelines.
lessons.remember: Mirroring is managed, near real-time replication of a source into read-only Delta tables in OneLake, with free replication compute.

lessons.title: Delta format in Fabric
lessons.summary: Delta Lake is Fabric's common table format.
lessons.remember: Everything in Fabric is Delta in OneLake; V-Order and regular compaction decide how fast it reads.

lessons.title: Data Factory pipelines
lessons.summary: A Fabric pipeline orchestrates work: it runs activities in order, with branching, loops, parameters and error paths.
lessons.remember: Fabric pipelines are ADF's orchestration model inside Fabric, minus datasets and SSIS, plus native Fabric activities.

lessons.title: Dataflows Gen2
lessons.summary: Dataflow Gen2 is low-code data preparation with Power Query, the same engine used in Excel and Power BI.
lessons.remember: Dataflow Gen2 is Power Query in Fabric: great for low-code shaping at moderate volume, costly for heavy lifting.

lessons.title: Copy job
lessons.summary: A Copy job is a Fabric item that moves data from a source to a destination without building a pipeline.
lessons.remember: Copy job is managed bulk and incremental copy with built-in state, the simplest way to land source tables in Fabric.

lessons.title: On-premises and VNet data gateways
lessons.summary: Fabric is a cloud service, so it needs a bridge to reach data behind a firewall: - The on-premises data gateway is Windows software you install on a machine inside your network.
lessons.remember: Use the on-premises gateway for data inside your own network and the VNet gateway for private Azure sources; Spark and Direct Lake do not go through gateways.

lessons.title: Notebooks in Fabric
lessons.summary: Fabric notebooks are the main place to write Spark code (PySpark, Spark SQL, Scala, SparkR) against OneLake.
lessons.remember: Fabric notebooks run Spark or plain Python against OneLake, with a default lakehouse and NotebookUtils for orchestration helpers.

lessons.title: Spark pools, environments and runtimes
lessons.summary: Fabric manages Spark clusters for you.
lessons.remember: Starter pools start fast, custom pools fit special needs, and environments pin the runtime and libraries your code needs.

lessons.title: Spark job definitions
lessons.summary: A Spark job definition is a Fabric item that runs a packaged Spark program, much like spark-submit.
lessons.remember: A Spark job definition is Fabric's spark-submit: a packaged program with arguments, environment and retries.

lessons.title: Spark performance features in Fabric
lessons.summary: Fabric adds several features on top of open-source Spark: - Native execution engine: runs supported Spark SQL operators in vectorised C++ (built on the open-source Velox and Apache Gluten projects) instead of the JVM.
lessons.remember: Fabric speeds Spark up with a native C++ engine and session sharing, but the fundamentals of partitioning and shuffle still decide performance.

lessons.title: Real-Time Intelligence overview
lessons.summary: Real-Time Intelligence is Fabric's workload for data in motion: telemetry, logs, clickstreams, IoT readings, change events.
lessons.remember: Real-Time Intelligence chains Eventstream to move, Eventhouse to store and query, dashboards to watch and Activator to act.

lessons.title: Eventstreams
lessons.summary: An Eventstream is a no-code pipeline for events.
lessons.remember: Eventstream connects, shapes and routes events without code, with at-least-once delivery.

lessons.title: Eventhouse and KQL databases
lessons.summary: An Eventhouse is a container for one or more KQL databases, the same engine as Azure Data Explorer.
lessons.remember: Eventhouse is Fabric's engine for fast queries over append-only event data, with an optional Delta copy in OneLake.

lessons.title: Activator
lessons.summary: Activator (formerly Data Activator; items still appear with the type name Reflex) watches data and acts when a condition is met.
lessons.remember: Activator turns conditions in data into alerts and actions, per tracked object.

lessons.title: Real-time dashboards
lessons.summary: A Real-Time Dashboard is a Fabric item whose tiles each run a KQL query against an Eventhouse, Azure Data Explorer or Azure Monitor.
lessons.remember: Real-time dashboards are KQL tiles for live operational monitoring; Power BI reports are for modelled business reporting.

lessons.title: Experiments and ML models
lessons.summary: Fabric's Data Science workload uses MLflow for machine learning bookkeeping, surfaced as two item types: - An experiment item groups training runs.
lessons.remember: Fabric experiments and models are MLflow under the hood, with PREDICT for batch scoring in Spark.

lessons.title: AutoML and ML tooling in Fabric
lessons.summary: AutoML automatically tries algorithms and hyperparameters and returns the best model by a chosen metric.
lessons.remember: Fabric AutoML (FLAML) finds a strong baseline model quickly, but the problem framing and data quality are still your job.

lessons.title: Copilot and AI features
lessons.summary: Fabric embeds generative AI in three ways: - Copilot inside workloads: generating Power Query steps in dataflows, building pipelines, writing SQL and KQL, creating Power BI report pages and summaries, and helping in note
lessons.remember: Copilot helps authors, data agents answer business questions over governed data, and AI functions enrich columns, all on paid capacity.

lessons.title: Semantic models
lessons.summary: A semantic model (formerly a Power BI dataset) is the business layer between data and reports.
lessons.remember: The semantic model is where business definitions and report security live; feed it a clean star schema.

lessons.title: Direct Lake
lessons.summary: Direct Lake is a semantic model storage mode that loads columns from Delta tables in OneLake directly into the VertiPaq engine when queries need them.
lessons.remember: Direct Lake reads OneLake Delta tables straight into Power BI's engine; keep tables compact and watch for fallback.

lessons.title: Reports, dashboards and apps
lessons.summary: Fabric includes the full Power BI service: - Reports: interactive pages of visuals on a semantic model, built in Power BI Desktop or the browser.
lessons.remember: Reports explore, paginated reports print, and apps distribute; security belongs in the model, not the report.

lessons.title: Governance model in Fabric
lessons.summary: Fabric governance is a delegated model: a small central team sets guardrails, and control is pushed down to the people closest to the data.
lessons.remember: Fabric governance flows from tenant to capacity and domain, to workspace, item and finally data-level security, and each layer has its own admin.

lessons.title: Tenant settings and admin portal
lessons.summary: Tenant settings switch Fabric features on or off for the organisation.
lessons.remember: Tenant settings switch features on or off for chosen groups and can be delegated to domains or capacities, but they do not secure data.

lessons.title: Domains
lessons.summary: A domain groups workspaces by business area: Finance, Sales, Manufacturing.
lessons.remember: Domains group workspaces by business area for discovery and delegated settings, but they are not a security boundary.

lessons.title: Workspace roles
lessons.summary: Every workspace has four roles, assigned to users, security groups, Microsoft 365 groups or service principals: Capability Admin Member Contributor Viewer --------------- Manage workspace, delete it, connect to Git Yes A
lessons.remember: Workspace roles are coarse: Contributor and above can read and change all data in the workspace, so design workspaces around who should see what.

lessons.title: Item permissions and sharing
lessons.summary: To give someone access to one item without a workspace role, you share it.
lessons.remember: Sharing grants Read only; ReadData opens the SQL path, ReadAll opens the Spark and file path, and write access needs a workspace role.

lessons.title: OneLake security
lessons.summary: OneLake security (which grew out of "OneLake data access roles") defines roles inside an item that grant access to specific tables, folders or schemas, optionally with row-level and column-level filters.
lessons.remember: OneLake security puts table, row and column permissions on the data itself, so SQL, Spark and Direct Lake all enforce the same rules.

lessons.title: Row, column and object level security
lessons.summary: Inside the Warehouse and SQL analytics endpoint, standard T-SQL security applies: - Object-level security: GRANT, DENY, REVOKE on tables, views, functions and procedures.
lessons.remember: T-SQL grants, RLS and masking protect the SQL path and model RLS protects the model; neither stops Spark reads on its own.

lessons.title: Sensitivity labels and DLP
lessons.summary: Sensitivity labels from Microsoft Purview Information Protection (for example Public, General, Confidential, Highly Confidential) can be applied to Fabric items.
lessons.remember: Sensitivity labels classify and travel downstream, DLP detects sensitive data, and protection policies restrict access by label.

lessons.title: Microsoft Purview and the OneLake catalog
lessons.summary: Two catalogs meet here: - The OneLake catalog is Fabric's built-in catalog, with three tabs.
lessons.remember: The OneLake catalog governs what is in Fabric; Purview governs the whole estate and scans Fabric into it.

lessons.title: Lineage and impact analysis
lessons.summary: Fabric captures item-level lineage automatically: which source feeds which pipeline or dataflow, which lakehouse feeds which semantic model, which model feeds which report.
lessons.remember: Fabric lineage is item-level: the lineage view shows a workspace, impact analysis shows everything downstream across workspaces.

lessons.title: Endorsement
lessons.summary: Endorsement marks items that people can trust.
lessons.remember: Promoted is the owner's claim, certified is a reviewer's approval, and master data marks the authoritative source.

lessons.title: Auditing and monitoring
lessons.summary: Fabric has several monitoring tools, each answering a different question: - Audit log (in Microsoft Purview Audit): who did what?
lessons.remember: Audit logs say who did what, the metrics app says how busy the capacity is, and the monitoring hub says whether jobs ran.

lessons.title: Git integration
lessons.summary: Git integration connects a Fabric workspace to a branch in a Git repository: Azure DevOps, GitHub or GitHub Enterprise (cloud versions only).
lessons.remember: Git integration versions Fabric item definitions per workspace branch; data and secrets stay out of Git.

lessons.title: Deployment pipelines
lessons.summary: A deployment pipeline promotes content between workspaces that represent stages, such as Development, Test and Production.
lessons.remember: Deployment pipelines promote item definitions between stage workspaces, with rules and autobinding to point each stage at its own data.

lessons.title: REST APIs and automation
lessons.summary: Everything you do in the Fabric portal can increasingly be automated: - Fabric REST APIs cover workspaces, items and item definitions, Git operations, deployment pipelines, job scheduling, the catalog and admin tasks (do
lessons.remember: REST APIs, the Fabric CLI, fabric-cicd and Terraform let you create and deploy Fabric content from code with service principals.

lessons.title: Lakehouse vs Warehouse (and Eventhouse)
lessons.summary: Fabric offers several stores that all keep data in OneLake.
lessons.remember: Pick the Lakehouse for Spark teams and all data shapes, the Warehouse for T-SQL teams needing transactions, and the Eventhouse for streaming and time series.

lessons.title: Fabric vs Databricks vs Snowflake
lessons.summary: The three platforms overlap heavily: all offer lakehouse-style storage on open formats, SQL warehousing, Spark or Spark-like processing, ML and AI features, and governance.
lessons.remember: Fabric centres on Microsoft and BI, Databricks on engineering and ML, Snowflake on SQL and sharing, and many estates combine them.

lessons.title: Capacity sizing and cost
lessons.summary: Sizing a Fabric capacity is iterative: 1.
lessons.remember: Estimate, prove with the Metrics app, separate risky workloads, reserve the base, and remember viewer licences below F64.

lessons.title: Migrating from legacy platforms to Fabric
lessons.summary: Typical sources and the Fabric tooling for each: - SQL Server, Synapse dedicated SQL pools (and Teradata metadata, preview) to Warehouse: the Migration Assistant for Fabric Data Warehouse imports a DACPAC, SQL scripts or
lessons.remember: Fabric's assistants translate code and schema, but a migration still needs a target design, parallel running and reconciliation.

lessons.title: When not to use Fabric
lessons.summary: Fabric is not the best answer everywhere.
lessons.remember: Avoid or limit Fabric where strict network isolation, multi-cloud, infrastructure control, tiny scale or low-latency serving dominate.

lessons.title: Batch, CDC and streaming ingestion (sample)
lessons.summary: There are three common ways to move data from source systems into an analytics platform: periodic batch copies, change data capture (CDC), and event streaming.
lessons.remember: Batch copies snapshots, CDC copies changes, streaming copies events.
